newsitem.title: NEPAL: Mountaineers ask Nepal to open new peaks.
newsitem.headline: Mountaineers ask Nepal to open new peaks.

text.p: Leading mountaineers on Thursday urged Nepal to open virgin peaks to relieve congestion around Mount Everest and lure more climbers to the kingdom, especially young Western climbers looking for adventure sports.

"People want to go to unknown areas. They have zero interest in well known mountain peaks along the well known routes," said Ian McNaught-Davis, president of the Berne-based Union Internationale des Associations d'Alpinisme.
McNaught-Davis was speaking in Kathmandu at an international climbers' meeting marking the 44th anniversary of the first ascent of Everest.

The conference was also attended by alpine bodies from India, China and Pakistan, which share the Himalayas with Nepal. Organisers said they wanted to work towards making mountaineering popular among young climbers.
Nepal has opened 142 Himalayan peaks, including the world's highest, the 8,848-metre (29,028-foot) Everest, to foreign climbers in five climbing seasons throughout the year.
In 1995, royalties paid by climbers, their expenses and other earnings from tourism totalled $117 million, or 18 percent of Nepal's net foreign exchange earnings.
Nepal is one of the world's 10 poorest countries. Tourism is its third largest source of foreign exchange.

There are more than 1,300 peaks which are over 6,000 metres (19,685 feet) high in the Nepal Himalayas, considered by Hindus to be the snowy abode of Lord Shiva, the god of destruction and reproduction.

Other climbers at the meeting urged Nepal to open new areas to decongest the Khumbhu region, where Everest is located. Khumbhu became popular after Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay first climbed Everest on May 29, 1953.
More than 700 climbers, from 167 expeditions sent by 43 countries, have climbed Everest so far. They include 41 women, and 90 climbers have reached the summit at least twice.
A total of 154 people have also been killed on Everest, which climbers can reach from either Nepal or Tibet.
Mountaineers at the conference expressed concerns over increasing pollution on Everest.
French climber Maurice Herzog asked Nepal to erect garbage disposal huts at the Everest base camp to destroy trash dumped by climbers on the mountain.

Herzog and another Frenchman, Louis Lachenal, climbed the 8,091-metre (26,545-ft) Annapurna I peak in June 1950, becoming the first mountaineers to reach the summit of a mountain more than 8,000 metres (22,154 feet) high.
Nepali officials said 60 percent of the revenue generated from mountaineering was spent on cleaning the mountains and on social and economic development activities in the area.
Last year, a government-sponsored cleaning expedition collected 2,000 kg (4,400 lbs) of garbage on Everest. Climbers said at least 15,000 kg (33,000 lbs) of decades-old trash remain to be collected.

Foreign climbers and their guides have left mounds of garbage -- empty oxygen and gas cylinders, stoves, tins, ropes, batteries and wooden and aluminium ladders -- since 1952 when the first climbing expedition was organised to Everest from the Nepali side.
